design.value: Alzheimer's Association-convened workgroup consensus criteria document (steering committee plus full workgroup) that updates the 2018 NIA-AA research framework; document_kind is consensus_statement rather than journal_article or systematic_review because it presents a convened workgroup's recommended diagnostic and staging criteria, not a study protocol or a systematic synthesis of a defined literature search
design.quote: The convening organization for these revised criteria is the AA. The AA identified a four‐person core leadership group for this effort (i.e., a steering committee) as well as a larger full workgroup.

n.quote: Four thousand eight hundred eighty‐nine individuals met these criteria. Of these, 4637 were symptomatic (i.e., CDR > 0) and 4390/4637 (95%) were Braak NFT stage III to VI
n.location: Rationale for diagnosis of AD by Core 1 biomarkers, NACC autopsy analysis

n_description.value: Participants in the December 2023 National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center autopsy data freeze who had CERAD moderate/frequent neuritic plaque density scores and had been assigned both a Braak NFT stage and a Clinical Dementia Rating. This is the workgroup's own supporting autopsy analysis, not enrollment in a trial; the document reports other, separate counts (123 Arizona cases, 252 asymptomatic NACC cases, 34 Mayo cases) which are not merged into this N.
n_description.quote: the December 2023 data freeze of the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) autopsy database for participants who had CERAD moderate/frequent neuritic plaque density scores and had been assigned both a Braak NFT stage and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)
n_description.location: Rationale for diagnosis of AD by Core 1 biomarkers

population.value: Individuals on the Alzheimer's disease continuum — people in whom AD has been diagnosed by Core 1 biomarkers, whether asymptomatic or symptomatic; the criteria explicitly do not apply to individuals who are not in the AD pathway
population.quote: Staging of AD applies only to individuals in whom the disease has been diagnosed by means of Core 1 biomarkers and does not apply to individuals who are not in the AD pathway.

biomarker_confirmation.value: Abnormality on specific Core 1 biomarkers: amyloid PET, CSF Aβ42/40, CSF p-tau181/Aβ42, CSF t-tau/Aβ42, or 'accurate' plasma assays (accuracy equivalent to approved CSF assays), or combinations of these
biomarker_confirmation.quote: Currently, we regard the following to be diagnostic of AD: amyloid PET, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Aβ 42/40, CSF p‐tau 181/Aβ 42, CSF t‐tau/Aβ 42, “accurate” plasma assays (defined below), or combinations of these.
biomarker_confirmation.location: BOX 2: The diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, Core 1 and Core 2 Alzheimer's disease biomarkers

cohorts: National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) autopsy database, December 2023 data freeze
Arizona Study of Aging and Neurodegenerative Disorders and Brain and Body Donation Program
Mayo Clinic Study on Aging and Alzheimer's Disease Research Center database

outcomes.name: Definition of Alzheimer's disease as a biological process beginning with AD neuropathologic change (ADNPC) in asymptomatic people
outcomes.quote: We define Alzheimer's disease (AD) to be a biological process that begins with the appearance of AD neuropathologic change (ADNPC) while people are asymptomatic.

outcomes.name: Core 1 biomarkers establish the diagnosis of AD
outcomes.quote: An abnormal Core 1 biomarker result is sufficient to establish a diagnosis of AD and to inform clinical decision making throughout the disease continuum.

outcomes.name: Composition of the Core 1 biomarker category (A, T1, hybrid ratios) and its timing relative to amyloid PET
outcomes.quote: Core 1 biomarkers become abnormal around the same time as amyloid PET, and are those in the A, T 1 , or hybrid ratio categories (Tables and ).

outcomes.name: Core 2 biomarkers (tau PET and T2 biofluids) provide prognostic information and increase confidence AD is contributing to symptoms
outcomes.quote: Later‐changing Core 2 biomarkers (biofluid and tau PET) can provide prognostic information, and when abnormal, will increase confidence that AD is contributing to symptoms.

outcomes.name: Split of the T biomarker category into T1 (early phosphorylated mid-region fragments) and T2 (tau PET and later tau fragments)
outcomes.quote: These observations led us to split the T biomarker category into two subcategories: T 1 (biofluid analytes of soluble tau fragments that may reflect a reaction to amyloid plaques
outcomes.location: BIOMARKER CATEGORIZATION, timing of T biomarkers

outcomes.name: Three broad biomarker categories: core ADNPC biomarkers, non-specific biomarkers, and biomarkers of non-AD copathology
outcomes.quote: We group biomarkers into three broad categories: core biomarkers of AD neuropathologic change (ADNPC), non‐specific biomarkers that are important in AD pathogenesis but are also involved in other brain diseases, and biomarkers of common non‐AD copathologies

outcomes.name: Addition of three new biomarker categories beyond AT(N): inflammation (I), vascular brain injury (V), alpha-synucleinopathy (S)
outcomes.quote: Accordingly, Tables and include three new biomarker categories: inflammatory/immune mechanisms (I), vascular brain injury (V), and alpha‐synucleinopathy (S).

outcomes.name: Minimum accuracy requirement of 90% for biomarkers used for clinical diagnosis
outcomes.effect_estimate: accuracy of 90% for identification of moderate/frequent neuritic plaques at autopsy or an approved surrogate, in the intended-use population
outcomes.quote: We recommend, as a minimum requirement, an accuracy of 90% for the identification of moderate/frequent neuritic plaques at autopsy (or an approved surrogate, which, at this point, would be amyloid PET or CSF) in the intended‐use population.
outcomes.location: BOX 2 / Anchoring Core 1 biomarkers for AD diagnosis to reference standards

outcomes.name: Four-stage biological staging scheme (stages A initial, B early, C intermediate, D advanced)
outcomes.quote: We propose a four‐stage scheme based on the sequence of events observed in natural history studies: stage A, initial changing biomarkers; stage B, early changing; stage C, intermediate changing; stage D, advanced changing

outcomes.name: Operationalization of biological stages by amyloid PET and tau PET (A+T2−, A+T2MTL+, A+T2MOD+, A+T2HIGH+)
outcomes.quote: Stage A ( initial )—abnormal amyloid PET with no uptake on tau PET (A+T 2 −); stage B ( early )—abnormal amyloid PET plus tau PET uptake that is restricted to medial temporal areas (A+T 2MTL +)
outcomes.location: Biological staging with amyloid PET and tau PET (Tables 3 and 4)

outcomes.name: Conceptual fluid-only biological staging scheme (Core 1 fluid, p-tau205, MTBR-tau243, non-phosphorylated mid-domain tau fragments)
outcomes.quote: This fluid‐only staging scheme is regarded as conceptual at present, and specifics of this conceptual scheme are likely to change given the rapidly changing nature of the fluid biomarker field.

outcomes.name: Six-stage numeric clinical staging scheme for individuals on the AD continuum
outcomes.quote: (1) biomarker evidence of AD in asymptomatic individuals; (2) transitional decline, which denotes the earliest detectable clinical symptoms that might be due to AD in individuals who are cognitively unimpaired

outcomes.name: Addition of clinical stage 0 for genetically determined, biomarker-negative, asymptomatic AD
outcomes.quote: Stage 0 represents part of the AD continuum and is defined as genetically determined AD (which includes ADAD or DSAD), in an individual who is biomarker negative and clinically asymptomatic

outcomes.name: Integrated biological and clinical staging scheme (clinical stages 0–6 in columns, biological stages A–D in rows)
outcomes.quote: we propose an integrated biological and clinical staging scheme in which clinical stages are denoted in the columns using the numeric six‐stage scheme plus stage 0. Biological stages are denoted in the rows.

outcomes.name: NACC autopsy analysis: proportion of symptomatic individuals with moderate/frequent neuritic plaques meeting intermediate/high ADNPC
outcomes.effect_estimate: 4390/4637 (95%) were Braak NFT stage III to VI
outcomes.quote: among symptomatic individuals, knowing only that someone has moderate/frequent plaques (i.e., an abnormal amyloid PET study) means that that individual will nearly always (95% of the time) qualify for a pathologic diagnosis of intermediate‐to‐high ADNPC
outcomes.location: Rationale for diagnosis of AD by Core 1 biomarkers

outcomes.name: Autopsy analyses in cognitively unimpaired individuals with moderate/frequent neuritic plaques (Arizona and NACC)
outcomes.effect_estimate: 107/123 (87%) in the Arizona series and 186/252 (74%) in NACC were Braak III–VI; 226/252 (91%) were Braak II–VI
outcomes.quote: we can conclude that while most (74%−87%) asymptomatic individuals with an abnormal amyloid PET scan (i.e., moderate/frequent neuritic plaques) will meet criteria for intermediate/high ADNPC at that time, a proportion will not.
outcomes.location: Rationale for diagnosis of AD by Core 1 biomarkers

outcomes.name: Mayo Clinic analysis of amyloid PET-positive cognitively unimpaired individuals who later progressed and came to autopsy
outcomes.effect_estimate: 32/34 (94%) received a neuropathological diagnosis of intermediate/high likelihood ADNPC
outcomes.quote: Of the 34 individuals who did meet these restrictive criteria, 32 (94%) received a neuropathological diagnosis of intermediate/high likelihood ADNPC.
outcomes.location: Rationale for diagnosis of AD by Core 1 biomarkers

outcomes.name: Prognostic value of PET-based biological staging: hazard ratios for progression from cognitively unimpaired to dementia
outcomes.effect_estimate: HR 1.5 for A+T2− (stage A), HR 5.6 for medial temporal tau PET uptake (stage B), HR 39.9 for neocortical tau PET uptake (stages C and D), relative to an A−T2− reference group; a 40-fold range in hazard ratios
outcomes.quote: the HR for progression from cognitively unimpaired to dementia was 1.5 for A+T 2 − individuals (stage A in our scheme), HR 5.6 for A+ individuals with tau PET uptake confined to the medial temporal lobe
outcomes.location: Caveats (biological staging), citing a large multi-cohort meta-analysis

outcomes.name: The A−T2+ biomarker profile is not consistent with a diagnosis of AD
outcomes.quote: The A−T 2 + biomarker profile is not consistent with a diagnosis of AD. First, this combination is rare., , Second, when it does occur, it is often due to quantitative values close to cutpoints

outcomes.name: T2N mismatch as an indirect indicator of non-AD copathology in a multimodal AT1T2NISV profile
outcomes.quote: The T 2 −N+ biomarker profile (i.e., T 2 N mismatch) therefore indicates the presence of neurodegeneration or neuronal injury due to a disease(s) other than AD.
outcomes.location: MULTIMODAL BIOMARKER PROFILES AND IDENTIFICATION OF COMORBID PATHOLOGIC CHANGE

primary_endpoint_status.explanation: This is a convened workgroup's consensus criteria document for diagnosing and staging Alzheimer's disease, not a study with a prespecified primary endpoint, so there is no endpoint to meet or miss.
primary_endpoint_status.quote: Our intent is to present objective criteria for diagnosis and staging AD, incorporating recent advances in biomarkers, to serve as a bridge between research and clinical care.

limitations: The criteria are not step-by-step clinical practice guidelines: 'These criteria are not intended to provide step-by-step clinical practice guidelines for clinical workflow or specific treatment protocols'

The criteria are presently operationalizable at some but by no means all centers, even among major medical institutions in high-income countries; the workgroup views them as a bridge between research and clinical care
Lack of certified biofluid reference methods and materials, except for CSF Aβ42 (Box 3)

PET, CSF and blood biomarkers are less sensitive than neuropathologic examination for detection of early/mild ADNPC, and disease staging by PET or fluid biomarkers is not equivalent to neuropathological staging (Box 3)
Thoroughly studied biomarkers are not available for all relevant diseases, so it cannot be known with certainty in vivo what diseases in addition to AD are present in any individual (Box 3)
The proportion of the cognitive deficit in any individual attributable to AD versus other neuropathologic entities cannot be known with certainty; only probabilistic estimates can be made (Box 3)
The fluid-only biological staging scheme is regarded as conceptual at present and its specifics are likely to change
Core 1 fluid biomarkers can establish that an individual is in biological stage A or higher but cannot at present discriminate between PET stages A–D

No blood-based biomarkers had received regulatory approval for any intended use at the time of writing, and diagnostic accuracy varies substantially among plasma p-tau and Aβ42/40 assays (0.6 to >0.9)
Specific proprietary fluid assays, PET ligands, and numeric cutpoints for staging are not specified in the document

Caveats for tau PET: off-target binding; medial temporal tauopathy does not always precede neocortical tauopathy, particularly in atypical presentations; anatomic ROIs are not fixed; the moderate versus high neocortical uptake cutpoint could be operationalized in different ways
The Centiloid scale is based on sporadic AD anatomic distribution, so determining A+ versus A− may need special consideration in autosomal dominant AD and Down syndrome AD
Much of the published AD biomarker data derive from highly educated, non-Hispanic White cohorts and have not been tested extensively in broadly representative populations
No confirmed disease-specific biomarkers currently exist for LATE, a common and clinically important contributor to late-life cognitive impairment
There is a dearth of available inflammatory/immune (I) biomarkers despite the importance of these mechanisms
It is unclear how best to categorize total tau in the current document when all evidence is considered
Feasibility of implementing these criteria in clinical practice varies across regions, even within World Bank-designated high-income countries

risk_of_bias.judgement: The workgroup was deliberately constituted to include industry representation alongside academic members, and the conflict of interest statement shows many members are employed by or hold equity in pharmaceutical and diagnostics companies whose products the criteria bear on.
risk_of_bias.quote: Members of the full workgroup were selected to provide a range of relevant scientific and clinical expertise; to achieve a representative sample of professional stakeholders; and to achieve a balance of academic and industry representation, sex/ethnicity, and geographic location.

risk_of_bias.domain: cohort representativeness of the supporting evidence
risk_of_bias.judgement: The document itself states that the biomarker evidence base underlying these criteria comes largely from highly educated, non-Hispanic White cohorts and has not been tested extensively in representative populations.
risk_of_bias.quote: Much of the published AD biomarker data have been derived from highly educated, non‐Hispanic White cohorts and these biomarkers have not yet been tested extensively in broadly representative populations.

risk_of_bias.domain: selection in the workgroup's own supporting autopsy analysis
risk_of_bias.judgement: The Mayo analysis supporting the claim that unimpaired amyloid-positive individuals would eventually meet ADNPC criteria used restrictive selection (amyloid PET positive while unimpaired, later progressed, and came to autopsy), which the document itself labels restrictive.
risk_of_bias.quote: Of the 34 individuals who did meet these restrictive criteria, 32 (94%) received a neuropathological diagnosis of intermediate/high likelihood ADNPC.

disagreements.question: Should Alzheimer's disease be defined by its biology or by its clinical syndrome?
disagreements.position: AD is defined by its biology; detection of AD neuropathologic change by biomarkers is equivalent to diagnosing the disease, and syndrome must be separated from etiology.
disagreements.quote: AD is defined by its unique neuropathologic findings; therefore, detection of AD neuropathologic change by biomarkers is equivalent to diagnosing the disease.

disagreements.question: Are cognitively unimpaired people with abnormal biomarkers 'at risk for' AD or do they already have it?
disagreements.position: They already have the disease; they are at risk only for symptoms, not for the disease itself.
disagreements.quote: Unimpaired individuals with abnormal biomarker test results are at risk for symptoms due to AD. They are not at risk for a disease they already have.

disagreements.question: Is 'at risk for AD' an appropriate label for unimpaired biomarker-positive individuals?
disagreements.position: No — such individuals should be categorized as AD clinical stage 1 or 2 because they already have the disease.
disagreements.quote: we would categorize these individuals as AD clinical stage 1 or 2, not as “at risk for AD” because they already have the disease.

disagreements.question: Is 'prodromal AD' the right term for biomarker-positive individuals with impairment short of dementia?
disagreements.position: No — such a person has the disease, not a prodrome of it; the workgroup's term is 'AD clinical stage 3'.
disagreements.quote: Our position is that such an individual has the disease, not a prodrome of the disease, and our terminology in this instance would be “AD clinical stage 3”

disagreements.question: Does a diagnosis of AD require both amyloid and tau biomarker abnormality (A+T+), as the 2018 research framework required?
disagreements.position: No — the T category is split into T1 and T2 and AD is now defined by abnormality on Core 1 biomarkers alone, which anchors in vivo onset to abnormal amyloid PET.
disagreements.attributed_to: Alzheimer's Association Workgroup (this document), departing from the 2018 NIA-AA research framework
disagreements.quote: In the 2018 research framework, an A+T+ biomarker profile was required for a designation of AD based on the AT(N) biomarker classification scheme.

disagreements.question: Are CSF and imaging biomarkers within the same AT(N) category interchangeable?
disagreements.position: Not always — the revised criteria break from the 2018 assumption of equivalence between imaging and biofluid biomarkers within a category.
disagreements.attributed_to: Alzheimer's Association Workgroup (this document), departing from the 2018 NIA-AA research framework
disagreements.quote: Ample evidence has accumulated that this is not always the case; therefore, in these revised criteria we break from the assumption of equivalence between imaging and biofluid biomarkers within a given biomarker category.

disagreements.question: Should plasma p-tau217, p-tau181 and p-tau231 be classified as biomarkers of amyloid beta plaques?
disagreements.position: No — the workgroup finds this conceptually difficult to accept because these are tau fragments that also correlate with tau proteinopathy, and resolves it by creating the T1/T2 subcategories.
disagreements.attributed_to: Alzheimer's Association Workgroup (this document), against a proposal in the field
disagreements.quote: plasma p‐tau 217, 181, and 231 have been proposed as biomarkers of Aβ plaques, but this is difficult to accept conceptually because these are tau fragments, not measures of the Aβ proteinopathy pathway.

disagreements.question: Does the fact that many people die with AD neuropathologic change but without symptoms mean the pathology is benign?
disagreements.position: No — mortality from unrelated causes should not be a criterion used to define what is and what is not a disease.
disagreements.quote: Mortality from unrelated diseases prior to symptom onset from AD should not be interpreted to indicate that ADNPC is benign.

disagreements.question: Should AD be diagnosed by biomarkers in cognitively unimpaired people in clinical practice?
disagreements.position: It can be, but the workgroup recommends against it for clinical purposes at this time, restricting such testing to observational or therapeutic research studies.
disagreements.quote: We highlight the distinction between can and should . AD can be diagnosed in asymptomatic individuals, but we do not believe this should be done for clinical purposes at this time.

disagreements.question: Should clinical symptoms serve as the reference standard for AD biomarker validation and approval?
disagreements.position: No — a biomarker that accurately detects ADNPC or a validated surrogate is sufficient to establish the diagnosis, because AD is defined by its biology.
disagreements.quote: Our position is that AD is defined by its biology and therefore a biomarker that can accurately detect ADNPC or a validated surrogate is sufficient to establish the diagnosis of the disease.

disagreements.question: Should genetic risk alleles such as APOE ε4 count as diagnostic of AD or define a stage?
disagreements.position: No — risk alleles are a risk factor only, because they do not indicate with certainty the presence or severity of ADNPC at a given time.
disagreements.quote: We therefore regard risk alleles as a risk factor for AD, not diagnostic of or a stage of AD.

disagreements.question: Should total tau remain in the neurodegeneration (N) biomarker category?
disagreements.position: The workgroup removes total tau from the fluid N category as a departure from 2018 and states that it is unclear how best to categorize this measure.
disagreements.attributed_to: Alzheimer's Association Workgroup (this document), departing from the 2018 NIA-AA research framework
disagreements.quote: The absence of total tau from the fluid biomarker N category (Tables and ) is a departure from the 2018 NIA‐AA research framework.

disagreements.question: Should neurodegeneration (N) and inflammation (I) biomarkers be part of the biological staging scheme?
disagreements.position: No — staging uses only core biomarkers, because N biomarkers do not always follow a stereotypical A+ to T2+ to N+ sequence.
disagreements.quote: We recommend a biological staging scheme that uses only core biomarkers. N biomarkers certainly add prognostic information;, , , however, the temporal relationships between core AD biomarkers and N biomarkers are inconsistent across individuals.

disagreements.question: Should blood-based biomarkers be treated as equivalent to PET and CSF for diagnosing AD?
disagreements.position: Yes, provided they meet the accuracy benchmark; the workgroup places qualifying blood-based markers on equal footing with established PET and CSF biomarkers.
disagreements.quote: Our position is that BBM that achieve this diagnostic performance benchmark should be considered on equal footing with established PET and CSF biomarkers for diagnosis of AD.

disagreements.question: Does removing amyloid to below PET detection with immunotherapy mean the disease has been eradicated or reverted to an earlier stage?
disagreements.position: No — the pathogenic process is still present, so the staging schemes should not be read as indicators of natural-history stage after treatment.
disagreements.quote: While Aβ may be reduced to subdetection levels on PET, this does not mean that the disease pathophysiology has been eradicated.

disagreements.question: Do anti-amyloid immunotherapy results support defining AD biologically?
disagreements.position: Yes — the workgroup reads the replicated link between amyloid PET reduction and clinical benefit as solid empiric support for a biological definition of AD.
disagreements.quote: These findings linking biology to clinical manifestations, which have been replicated across independent therapeutic programs,, , , provide solid empiric support for a biological definition of AD.
